summary.text: The Scientific Revolution of the 16th and 17th centuries in Europe was an irreversible break with earlier natural philosophy that changed how the natural world was investigated.
The New Science was more mechanistic, more integrated with mathematics, and focused on gathering and interpreting new evidence.
The period is often said to have begun in 1543 with books by Vesalius and Copernicus, and it culminated with Newton's Principia in 1687.

facts.label: Usual start
facts.value: 1543, with books by Vesalius and Copernicus

facts.label: Printing press
facts.value: Introduced in Europe by Gutenberg in the 1440s

facts.label: Where it began
facts.value: A few Western European countries, for about two hundred years

facts.label: Popularized by
facts.value: Historian Herbert Butterfield, in Origins of Modern Science

items.prompt: A scholar around 1500 pictures an unchanging heavens above an Earth at the center, made of four elements. Whose universe is this?

options.label: Copernicus's, with the Sun in the middle
Galileo's, built from telescope observations
Aristotle's, with a geocentric hierarchy
Newton's, unified by one set of laws

items.explain: Aristotle's universe was geocentric and hierarchical, with an imperfect terrestrial region surrounded by an unchanging celestial realm.

items.prompt: What did the movable type press give scholars in different countries that manuscripts could not?

options.label: Freedom from ever consulting ancient texts
A shared set of diagrams and texts to study
Separate national versions of each treatise
An end to comparing their own observations

items.explain: Printing meant scholars in different countries studied the same diagrams and read the same texts, and could compare their observations with those of fellow scholars.

items.prompt: Where did the first historical record of the telescope's invention appear?

options.label: A treatise by a natural philosopher
A founding charter of the Royal Society
A letter published by Vespucci
A patent filed by a spectacle maker

items.explain: The record did not appear in a work of natural philosophy but in a patent filed by a spectacle maker.

items.prompt: Why did the discovery of the Americas shake European trust in Ptolemy's astronomy?

options.label: He was trusted on astronomy and geography, but his maps lacked the Americas
His astronomy was built on voyages to the Americas
Sailors found stars his catalogue had left out
He had predicted the Americas in the wrong place

items.explain: Ptolemy's maps had no Americas, and he was also considered the leading authority on astronomy, so the surprise questioned his astronomy's reliability.

items.prompt: A friend says Copernicus, Galileo and Newton owed nothing to earlier thinkers. How fair is that?

options.label: Fair, since they rejected all earlier learning
Fair, since universities taught only new ideas
Unfair, since they studied at medieval universities and acknowledged debts
Unfair, since they simply continued Aristotle unchanged

items.explain: They broke with Renaissance Aristotelianism, yet all studied at universities founded in the High Middle Ages and acknowledged debts to earlier scholars.

items.prompt: Francis Bacon's confident announcement of modern scientific progress inspired people to create what?

options.label: Scientific societies such as the Royal Society
A new universal language for scholars
Printing houses for religious texts
Observatories along trade routes

items.explain: Bacon's announcement inspired the creation of scientific societies such as the Royal Society.
